items.title: Aluminium Gives Up Its War Premium, Copper Stays Elevated

events.article_text:
Oil Prices Surge Above $111 as Houthis Strike Saudi Targets

Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com.

LME Week 2026 kicked off in London on Monday, with industry leaders focused on the macroeconomic outlook for base metals, AI and energy transition demand, as well as critical mineral supply chain resilience. This year's discussions have come at a time when the London Metal Exchange is robustly healthy, recording a 16% year-on-year increase in average daily turnover from January through September.

Standard Chartered's commodity analysts expect mixed results for base metals in the coming months. Prices will follow macroeconomic conditions (risk appetite, Fed rate policy, U.S. dollar moves and China's economic activity), geopolitics, U.S. copper tariff uncertainty and supply.

The analysts said uncertainty over metal-specific tariffs continues to cause price volatility, premium swings and inventory dislocations. Supply issues remain important drivers as well: output disruptions, mining quotas, smelter power contracts, sulphur tightness and wage renegotiations.

Standard Chartered's near- and mid-term projections for each base metal follow.

Stanchart expect prices to remain at elevated levels for the rest of 2026, buoyed by supply stresses and US copper tariff uncertainty which remains the key event risk.

The analysts have upgraded their average copper price forecast to $13,674 per ton in 2026 and $13,210 per ton in 2027, up from previous projections of $13,472/t in 2026 and $12,875/t in 2027.

Copper prices are up 16% YTD, having set a series of all-time highs throughout the year. Meanwhile, the nearby LME spread has been mostly in backwardation since July, with only a brief move to contango in mid-September. In addition to copper-specific factors--including uncertainty over the pending U.S. tariff review, physical inventory dislocations and supply challenges--prices have been driven by macro dynamics such as risk sentiment, USD moves and Fed policy expectations.

Beyond macro drivers, Stanchart sees two key dynamics supporting elevated copper prices in near-term. The first is continued uncertainty over the U.S. copper tariff review, with the Trump administration yet to provide an update on whether refined copper imports--which have been exempt so far--will become subject to tariffs.

The second is supply, and Stanchart sees it intensifying. Upside risks to copper prices include further tightening of ex-U.S. inventories and optimism over AI demand. Downside risks include downgrades to global growth expectations, weaker risk appetite, geopolitical developments, further U.S. dollar strength and hawkish Fed policy.

Stanchart notes that the premium of Comex over LME copper has narrowed. The physical dislocation in exchange inventories continues. Comex inventories reached a fresh record high of 790.4kt, partly because of persistent U.S. copper tariff uncertainty. The pace of builds has picked up since mid-September, when inventories showed intermittent daily declines and modest builds.

LME copper inventories have continued to decline in October, as have cancelled warrants. On-warrant inventories rose to 140kt, their highest in a month. SHFE inventories remain low overall. Strong spot demand from China shows in the Yangshan copper import premium, which has risen to $137/t, its highest since November 2022.

Chile's copper-mine output fell 12.8% Y/Y in August to its lowest monthly level since February 2011. Output is down 7.8% Y/Y in the year to date, and Stanchart projects that Chile's 2026 copper production will decline by slightly more than 5% Y/Y before rebounding in 2027.

Labour tensions have risen in Chile as wage renegotiations proceed. A strike has been averted at the Escondida mine, the world's largest. A strike at the Centinela mine has ended after mediation talks led to the acceptance of a renegotiated wage offer.

In contrast, Stanchart has lowered its aluminum price forecasts to reflect better supply prospects driven by a faster-than-expected recovery of Middle East supply, the ramp-up in Indonesian output, robust China smelter production and Europe restarts. The analysts now expect prices to average $3,249/t in 2026 ($3,318/t previously) and $3,001/t in 2027 ($3,199/t

Aluminium prices have erased the entire Middle East supply risk premium. They posted their first sub-$3,000/t closes of 2026 on Oct. 14-15 before moving back above that level the next trading day, and the drop to recent lows returned prices to their pre-conflict levels.

Full resumption of GCC supply remains uncertain. The Strait of Hormuz is still disrupted, freight costs are higher and alternate routes face logistical problems.

Prices fell on three developments that have eased concerns, for now, about the loss of GCC units: strong production growth in China and Indonesia, robust Chinese exports of semi-finished aluminium products (semis), and restarts at European smelters.

China’s production has been rising on record margins, with operating utilization rates running at an all-time high at 98.5%. Data from China’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) shows domestic output at 3.98 million tonnes (Mt) in August, with YTD output hitting 31.1Mt, up 3.9%Y/Y. China’s aluminium smelters have been maximizing output on high margins, moving above the official capacity cap of 45 Mt. Further, as China imposes a 30% export tax on primary exports, the surge in aluminium exports this year has been driven by aluminium semis exports. China customs data for September shows that unwrought aluminium and semis exports rose 25.9%Y/Y to 656 kt, a three-month high. Meanwhile, exports are up 17.8%Y/Y to 5.32 Mt.

analysis.tldr: Global copper prices are heading higher due to mine troubles and US tariff worries, which could mean pricier wiring and appliances for Indian consumers, while aluminium gets cheaper because of rising production in China and Indonesia.
the_story: Standard Chartered commodity analysts upgraded their average copper price forecasts to $13,674 per ton for 2026 and $13,210 per ton for 2027.
Copper prices have been supported by severe supply challenges, including Chile's copper-mine output falling 12.8% year-on-year in August.
In contrast, aluminium prices have dropped back down to pre-conflict levels, erasing the Middle East supply risk premium.
Aluminium supply pressures eased due to faster-than-expected recoveries in the Middle East, increased output in Indonesia, and robust production in China.
analysis.what_happened: Global metal markets are moving in opposite directions because of supply changes. Copper prices are staying high and breaking records due to mine production drops in Chile and ongoing worries about potential US import taxes. Meanwhile, aluminium prices dropped below $3,000 per ton because factories in China, Indonesia, and Europe managed to produce much more metal than expected.
analysis.analogy: It is like two different fruit stalls in a market: one stall has fewer apples because bad weather ruined the harvest (copper), so prices go up; the other stall has extra oranges arriving from neighboring farms (aluminium), so those prices drop.
why_it_matters_india: Global copper prices rise due to foreign mine shortages and US tariff uncertainty.
Indian manufacturing industries that buy raw copper for electrical wires and electronics face higher material costs.
Indian companies pass these higher production costs down to everyday consumers, raising the price of electrical goods.
At the same time, cheaper global aluminium helps lower input costs for Indian construction and packaging sectors.

impacts.rationale: Supply issues in Chile and US tariff worries are keeping global prices elevated, making electrical wiring and electronics more expensive for everyday consumers.
Surging production from China and Indonesia has erased war risk premiums, which is good news for Indian construction and packaging industries needing cheap metal.
Higher global copper and metal trends generally boost earnings for major mining and metal-producing companies in India, which is good for shareholders.

watch_next: Decisions from the US administration regarding whether they will place tariffs on refined copper imports
Updates on labour negotiations and mine production numbers coming out of Chile
analysis.caveats: Unexpected global economic slowdowns or sudden shifts in Chinese factory demand could rapidly alter these metal price trends.

The differing opinions highlight the complexities of achieving growth while managing inflation effectively.

analysis.tldr: Borrowing money is going to stay expensive because the central bank is keeping interest rates high to fight rising prices.
the_story: The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) Monetary Policy Committee (the group that decides interest rates) raised the benchmark repo rate (the interest rate the RBI charges commercial banks) by 25 basis points (0.25 percentage points) to fight rising inflation (general increase in prices).
Governor Sanjay Malhotra pointed out that inflation has spread widely, with many everyday goods and commodities seeing price rises of over 4%.
Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta noted that global supply shocks (sudden disruptions in getting goods from abroad) are pushing up inflation forecasts.
External members of the committee worried that raising interest rates too aggressively could slow down overall economic growth.
analysis.what_happened: The RBI raised its main lending rate by 0.25% because prices across many goods are rising faster than comfortable, and global supply problems are making things worse. This means the central bank has put any plans to lower interest rates on hold to cool down inflation.
analysis.analogy: It is like a strict parent hiding the car keys and turning off your allowance because you are spending too fast — they are making money harder to get so you stop buying things and prices stop going up.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI raises its benchmark repo rate to fight widening inflation.
Commercial banks face higher borrowing costs and pass them on to consumers.
Loans for homes, cars, and businesses become more expensive to service.
Higher borrowing costs slow down consumer spending and cool economic growth.

impacts.target: Home and car loan EMIs (monthly loan payments)
impacts.rationale: When the RBI raises its benchmark rate, banks make loans more expensive, which means higher monthly payments for borrowers — bad for everyday people carrying debt.
Higher interest rates cool down spending in the economy, which helps bring rising prices back under control — good for consumers in the long run.
More expensive loans hurt company profits and slow down business growth, which can make stock prices drop — tough for investors in the short term.

watch_next: Upcoming statements from RBI officials on whether more rate hikes are coming
Monthly inflation data to see if prices are finally slowing down
analysis.caveats: This card relies on text from the article provided, but note that the text also contained promotional clutter and unrelated headlines from the source page.

analysis.tldr: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI [India's central bank that manages money and interest rates]) has clarified its new rules on currency protection, which could help banks start trading dollars smoothly again and steady the Indian rupee.
the_story: The Reserve Bank of India issued clarifications on recent measures meant to support the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
Banks had held back on quoting dollar-rupee forwards (agreements to buy or sell foreign currency at a set price in the future) because of confusion over new transaction rules and cash margins.

The RBI's original measures included redirecting oil companies' (firms that import crude oil) dollar purchases and levying cash reserve requirements (money banks must keep parked safely with the central bank).
These rules had created uncertainty and confusion in financial markets.
analysis.what_happened: The Reserve Bank of India stepped in to explain its recent steps aimed at protecting the Indian rupee. Banks had stopped trading certain currency contracts due to confusion over the new rules and cash requirements, creating stress in financial markets.
analysis.analogy: It is like a traffic police officer putting up a new, confusing sign at a busy crossing that makes all drivers stop out of fear of breaking the rule, until the officer steps out to clearly explain how to drive through.
why_it_matters_india: RBI issues new rules to support the rupee -> creates confusion among banks
Banks pause dollar-rupee forward contracts -> trading slows down in the market
RBI provides clarifications -> banks understand the new requirements better
Banks resume normal trading -> market uncertainty drops and currency markets stabilize

impacts.rationale: Clarifications help banks manage currency trades smoothly again, which can help support the rupee's value against sudden drops.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Clearer rules reduce market panic, which generally keeps borrowing costs stable for the government.

watch_next: Whether banks actually restart quoting dollar-rupee forward contracts smoothly
Any further statements from the Reserve Bank of India on foreign exchange rules
analysis.caveats: The article text is very brief, so market reactions depend heavily on how banks interpret the RBI's clarifications in practice.

items.title: Best of Opinion: India must step up to reshape WTO to benefit Global South
items.summary: Today's editorials and columns examine delays in satellite broadband approvals, highway construction safety, India's role in WTO reforms, the RBI's rupee strategy and the struggle for women's rights

analysis.tldr: Opinions suggest India should take a leading role in changing global trade rules to better support developing nations, which could shape future trade costs for Indian businesses.
the_story: An opinion piece argues that India must step up to reshape the WTO (World Trade Organization, the global body that sets rules for international trade).
The stated goal of this reshaping is to benefit the Global South (developing countries, mostly in Asia, Africa, and Latin America).
analysis.what_happened: The article text is not available, but the headline argues that India needs to take a more active role in reforming global trade rules at the World Trade Organization to better support developing countries.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of shopkeepers needing one strong voice to negotiate better wholesale prices with the market landlord on everyone's behalf.
why_it_matters_india: India advocates for developing nations at international trade forums like the WTO.
Changes to global trade rules can alter export and import costs for Indian industries.
This impacts how competitive Indian products are in the global market.
Ultimately, shifting trade policies can influence economic growth and domestic job markets.

impacts.rationale: Better global trade terms could help Indian export companies grow, which is generally good for stock prices, but this is an opinion piece with no immediate market impact.
Smoother international trade relations generally help service and tech businesses, though trade bodies focus more on physical goods and agriculture.

watch_next: Official statements from Indian trade ministers regarding WTO reforms
Upcoming global trade meetings involving developing nations
analysis.caveats: Only the headline was available, so the specific policy recommendations and details of the opinion piece are unknown.

analysis.tldr: When global investors feel nervous, they rush to safe assets like Japanese bonds, which can pull foreign money away from emerging markets like India.
the_story: Japanese government bond yields (the interest rate the government pays to borrow) fell to multiweek lows on Thursday.
The 10-year Japanese bond yield dropped to 2.88%.
This drop was driven by geopolitical tensions and inflation concerns, which boosted safe-haven demand (the urge to put money in ultra-safe places when the world feels risky).
Investors are waiting for the Bank of Japan's policy meeting while weighing potential rate hikes and global economic uncertainties.
analysis.what_happened: Japanese bond yields dropped because people around the world became worried about global safety and rising prices. To keep their money safe, investors rushed to buy Japanese government bonds. When many people want to buy bonds, the government doesn't need to offer high interest to attract them, so the yield (the return investors get) falls.
analysis.analogy: It is like a sudden heavy rainstorm sending everyone running for the nearest covered porch—the porch gets packed, and people crowd in because it feels safe.
why_it_matters_india: Global investors seek out safe havens like Japanese government bonds when geopolitical tensions rise.
This shift in mood can cause global funds to look away from developing markets.
If foreign investors pull money out of India to buy safe-haven assets abroad, it puts pressure on Indian financial markets.
A general tightening of global financial conditions makes it costlier for Indian companies to raise money overseas.

impacts.rationale: If global panic grows and foreign investors pull money out of India, local stock prices can face downward pressure — generally bad for everyday equity investors.
When foreign capital leaves emerging markets, the local currency often weakens, making imported items like crude oil more expensive for India.

watch_next: The upcoming policy meeting announcements from the Bank of Japan
Any updates on global geopolitical tensions
analysis.caveats: The article text contains a mix of unrelated promotional content, so the analysis is built strictly from the headline details about Japanese bond yields and the upcoming Bank of Japan meeting.

events.headline: China’s AI Industry Brings Both Gains and Challenges for Its Fragile Economy

items.title: China’s AI Industry Brings Both Gains and Challenges for Its Fragile Economy
items.summary: China’s exports are surging, driven by AI-related technologies. National security-driven export bans could change that.

events.article_text:
China is attracting global interest and achieving record-breaking export growth as a trailblazer in the field of artificial intelligence (AI). However, the sector’s growing importance for China’s economy is a double-edged sword. The delicacy of the ongoing AI race, coupled with its national security implications, could lead to curbs on the sharing of certain technologies, casting new doubt on the frontier as an economic driver.

China’s exports are growing at a phenomenal rate, recording a 36.3 percent year-on-year boost in September to reach $447.18 billion. That’s the highest growth level for Chinese exports since 2021, and even then figures were somewhat unreliable due to the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

September’s figures extended a positive run. China’s exports grew 25 percent year-on-year in August. In both months, high-tech trade was a critical contributor to the surging growth. China’s semiconductor exports grew more than 108 percent over the past month, and automatic data processing machine shipments, recorded a boost of 55 percent.

The AI industry has been providing economic tailwinds for China, bolstered by government initiatives to support the development of the technology domestically. In turn, China’s tech-focused exports have helped to support the national economy. However, it appears that China is mulling placing new bans on exports focusing on emerging technologies. That includes AI as well as biotechnology and solar power.

In recent days, China has unveiled a draft plan to establish a fresh series of export bans that will impact 14 different forms of technology. The notice, issued by China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology, proposes bans or restrictions that cover 40 technologies in total. The Ministry of Commerce has claimed that the implementation of export bans is necessary to reinforce security while preventing misuse and abuse.

If implemented, those curbs could significantly impact the nation’s ongoing export boom. Critically, the restrictions would see domestic AI models with parameter counts of 2 trillion or more excluded from exports. Parameter counts are important measures of the learning capacity of models, and controlling higher-end models is likely to be China’s way of maintaining an edge in a highly competitive buildout. Both of China’s leading AI models – Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.8-Max – exceed parameter counts of 2 trillion, meaning that their export could be banned entirely.

However, it’s worth noting that foreign businesses and users would still be able to use AI models via front-end software like APIs, websites, or cloud apps, just so long as the underlying core technology remains hosted securely inside China.

There’s also the potential for foreign-owned businesses to enter foreign-trade zones like Beijing to maintain their access to Chinese AI technology. However, the intricacies of market entry in China mean that higher degrees of access to domestic AI tools aren’t assured forever.

As China’s government considers tighter restrictions on technology-related exports, it will have to confront the economic implications. The nation has secured significant growth off the back of its strength in AI. Alongside the nation’s export strength, growing interest in Chinese AI from overseas is helping to transform both trade and the economy on a fundamental level. It’s also supporting China’s economic ties with other countries in a way that boosts global integration.

Chinese exports of integrated circuits surged 99.1 percent year-on-year in the first three quarters of 2026. Other sectors of technology, such as computer parts and accessories, have seen Chinese exports more than triple over the same period.

Even so, the latest figures show that China’s economy expanded 4.4 percent in the third quarter. That’s below the government target of between 4.5 percent and 5 percent GDP growth for the year – China’s lowest growth target in decades.

Although AI exports have helped to support the economy, Beijing is still struggling to address its sinking real estate sector in the post-pandemic landscape. Multiple geopolitical stresses and macroeconomic headwinds linked to both trade rows and global conflicts have stifled growth in a way that has absorbed China’s high-tech export success story. The prospect of tighter controls over AI exports could create fresh pressures for an economy that’s already facing severe challenges.

At this stage, it’s important to note that China’s AI export bans would largely be limited to the distribution of its high-end models, meaning that we can still expect a sustained upturn in high-tech exports throughout the final quarter 2026. But with AI helping to strengthen China’s international ties with other countries, stronger restrictions on its frontier technology could stunt its growth at a time when the economy appears set to miss its annual targets.

For a nation that’s still seeking to plot its recovery from a deep real estate crisis, AI has emerged as a major economic opportunity. However, China’s strong stance on protecting national security could create more economic disruption, making the road to 5 percent growth even more challenging.

analysis.tldr: China considering bans on exporting top-tier AI models could alter global tech supply chains, potentially shifting tech investments toward alternative markets like India.
the_story: China's exports hit $447.18 billion in September, growing 36.3 percent year-on-year, driven by high-tech trade like a 108 percent jump in semiconductor exports.
China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology unveiled a draft plan proposing bans or restrictions on 40 technologies, including AI, biotechnology, and solar power.

The proposed curbs would ban the export of advanced domestic AI models with parameter counts of 2 trillion or more, which includes leading models like Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 and Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-Max.
Despite the high-tech boom, China's overall economy expanded by only 4.4 percent in the third quarter, missing the government's target of 4.5 to 5 percent due to a struggling real estate sector.
Foreign users can still access Chinese AI via cloud apps or front-end software as long as the core technology stays hosted in China, or by entering special foreign-trade zones like Beijing.
analysis.what_happened: China's exports surged due to high-tech goods like AI and semiconductors, providing a boost to its otherwise slowing economy. However, the Chinese government is proposing new bans on exporting its most advanced AI models to protect national security, which could complicate its growth at a time when the broader economy is missing targets because of a property market crisis.
analysis.analogy: It is like a popular bakery making record profits selling its secret-recipe cakes abroad, but suddenly deciding to stop shipping the best cakes overseas to keep them local, even though the bakery's main dining room is struggling with empty tables.
why_it_matters_india: China restricts the export of its top-tier artificial intelligence technology ->
Global tech companies and researchers look for alternative tech partners and supply chains ->
Capital and technology investments flow toward alternative emerging markets like India ->
Indian technology and manufacturing sectors experience greater global attention and potential inflows

impacts.rationale: Potential restrictions on Chinese tech exports could push global clients to seek alternative software and AI development partners in countries like India, which is generally good for Indian IT firms.
If foreign investors pull back from restricted Chinese markets and reallocate funds to other emerging markets like India, local stock indices could see a boost.
Potential curbs on Chinese solar power technologies could alter global equipment prices, indirectly impacting domestic renewable costs and overall inflation.

watch_next: Whether China formally implements the draft export bans on the 40 targeted technologies
Quarterly export and GDP numbers from China to see if the high-tech boom offsets property sector troubles
analysis.caveats: The export curbs mentioned are currently just a draft plan and have not yet been fully implemented by the Chinese government.

events.headline: AI boom and trade resilience to Middle East crisis lift outlook, but gains to be uneven

items.title: AI boom and trade resilience to Middle East crisis lift outlook, but gains to be uneven
items.summary: Global trade proved more resilient than expected in the first half of 2026 despite the disruption caused by the Middle East conflict, as supply chains adapted and strong investment in artificial intelligence provided a powerful boost to goods trade. However, the resilience was not uniform, with services trade and some regions more exposed to the effects of the conflict. WTO economists have therefore raised the forecast for merchandise trade growth in 2026 while lowering the outlook for services trade.

events.article_text:
According to the latest "Global Trade Outlook and Statistics" released on 8 October, merchandise trade volume is now expected to grow by 3.9% in 2026, up from the March forecast of 1.9%, before increasing further to 4.1% in 2027 (see Chart 1). The revision reflects evidence that global supply chains adapted to disruptions in energy and fertilizer markets, while strong investment in AI-related infrastructure boosted trade in AI-enabling goods. Commercial services trade growth is expected to remain positive, although prospects have moderated due to the impact of the Middle East conflict on transport and international travel. Services trade volume is expected to grow by 3.3% in 2026, down from 4.8% in the March forecast, before rising by 6.4% in 2027.

Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said: "The numbers reflect trade resilience in action. When disruptions strike, an integrated world economy and a rules-based trading system provide economies flexibility to keep essential products flowing to businesses and households that need them. Nevertheless, some have felt the shock more than others, and not everyone can access emerging opportunities like AI. It is essential to ensure that the rules-based trading system continues to absorb shocks and bridge gaps so that opportunities are open to all."

Merchandise trade volume grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2026, exceeding expectations despite the disruption caused by the Middle East conflict. The performance reflected the ability of supply chains to adapt to shocks affecting energy, fertilizer and transport markets. Although crude oil exports from the Middle East fell by roughly 24% and liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports by 47% in the first half of 2026, increased shipments from other suppliers helped limit the decline in global exports to around 6% for crude oil and just 1% for LNG. Fertilizer markets also adjusted despite severe disruption, with global imports of nitrogenous fertilizers only 2.8% below recent averages and phosphatic fertilizer imports 2.2% higher as alternative suppliers stepped in. Meanwhile, trade flows were rerouted through alternative ports and corridors. Global container throughput remained resilient, rising 3.9% year-to-date through July.

Strong demand linked to AI investment more than offset the negative effects of the conflict in the Middle East. Demand for AI-enabling goods such as semiconductors and servers accounted for 47% of global merchandise trade growth in the first half of 2026, and trade in these products rose by 67% year-on-year, accelerating from the already rapid expansion seen in 2024 and 2025.

Commercial services trade grew by 14% year-on-year in value terms in the first quarter of 2026 and 10% in the second quarter. Growth slowed in the second quarter as the Middle East conflict disrupted transport and travel services, two sectors that depend heavily on the region's role as a global hub. Transport services were affected by the reorganization of shipping routes and sharply higher freight costs. Travellers' expenditure abroad increased by just 5% year-on-year in the second quarter, down from 15% in the first quarter. International tourist arrivals fell by 0.8% in the second quarter and were only 0.4% higher in the first half of the year overall according to data from the United Nations World Tourism Organization, reflecting a contraction in international tourist arrivals.

Despite these headwinds, other commercial services, particularly digitally delivered services, remained comparatively resilient and continued to support overall services trade growth. Computer services exports, one of the fastest-growing segments of services trade, rose by 18% year-on-year in the first quarter and an estimated 12% in the second quarter, helping to offset weakness in transport and travel services. Financial services exports likewise grew, by 14% year-on-year in the second quarter.

The report includes an analytical chapter on trade in AI-enabling goods, examining how the AI investment boom is reshaping global trade patterns, regional specialization and the geography of demand and supply.

Given stronger-than-expected merchandise trade growth in the first half of 2026, WTO economists now expect world merchandise trade volume to increase by 3.9% in 2026 and 4.1% in 2027, while global GDP growth is forecast at 2.6% and 2.9%, respectively (see Table 1).

AI-related investment is expected to remain a major driver of merchandise trade through 2027. Global AI infrastructure spending is projected to increase by at least 30% in 2026. Current market projections suggest AI capital expenditure will continue to rise by a further 10-20% in 2027. The conflict in the Middle East is expected to weigh on trade in 2026 through higher energy prices and disruptions to transport routes.

Regional trade prospects remain uneven. In 2026, Asia is expected to record the fastest merchandise export growth (9.9%), followed by North America (5.7%), Africa (5.6%) and South America (3.4%). Export performance is projected to remain weak in Europe (-0.1%) and to contract sharply in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) (-3.9%) and the Middle East (-17.2%), reflecting the impact of the ongoing conflict and associated disruptions to trade flows. On the import side, Asia (9.5%), Africa (8.9%) and the CIS (8.8%) are expected to post the strongest growth, while North America (1.4%) and Europe (0.5%) are likely to see only modest increases and the Middle East is forecast to record a steep decline (-15.4%).

The outlook for commercial services trade has weakened since the March forecast as the conflict in the Middle East continues to disrupt transport and travel services. WTO economists now expect commercial services trade volume to grow by 3.3% in 2026, down from the previous forecast of 4.8%, before rebounding to 6.4% in 2027 (see Table 2). Transport and travel are expected to record only modest growth this year, reflecting higher energy costs, disru

analysis.tldr: A global boom in artificial intelligence and resilient supply chains are lifting world trade forecasts, which could mean more demand for India's computer services but also higher transport costs from ongoing conflicts.
the_story: According to the WTO's 'Global Trade Outlook and Statistics' released on 8 October, global merchandise trade volume is expected to grow by 3.9% in 2026 and 4.1% in 2027.
Global supply chains successfully adapted to disruptions, with alternative suppliers limiting the decline in Middle Eastern crude oil and LNG exports.
Demand for AI-enabling goods like semiconductors and servers drove 47% of global merchandise trade growth in the first half of 2026, with trade in these items jumping 67% year-on-year.

Commercial services trade growth slowed to 3.3% for 2026 due to Middle East conflict disruptions affecting transport and international travel, though computer services exports rose 18% in the first quarter and 12% in the second.
analysis.what_happened: The World Trade Organization raised its global trade growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027. This happened because global supply chains adapted smoothly to Middle East disruptions, and massive investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure created huge demand for tech hardware.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major highway getting blocked by roadwork, but delivery drivers quickly finding side streets so packages still arrive, while a sudden massive craving for a specific snack creates a boom for grocery store suppliers.
why_it_matters_india: Global trade volume grows -> demand for manufactured goods and digital services rises worldwide.
AI infrastructure spending surges -> global appetite for technology and software increases.
Computer services exports rise globally (including 18% in Q1) -> benefits countries with strong tech service sectors like India.
Middle East conflict disrupts transport and travel -> pushes up shipping costs and travel expenses, creating mixed pressures on global inflation.

impacts.rationale: Globally, computer services exports are growing strongly (up 12-18%), which is generally good for earnings prospects of Indian technology exporters.
Middle East conflicts are disrupting transport routes and shipping, leading to sharply higher freight costs which makes importing and exporting goods pricier for businesses.
Stronger global merchandise trade and high demand for AI hardware provide a positive backdrop for export-oriented sectors, supporting overall market sentiment.

watch_next: Updates on Middle East transport route disruptions and shipping costs
Global capital expenditure announcements on artificial intelligence infrastructure
analysis.caveats: If the Middle East conflict intensifies further, it could disrupt energy markets and transport networks more severely than anticipated, dampening global trade growth.

events.headline: UNEP: Opportunity has ‘been lost’ to meet 1.5C warming limit without ‘overshoot’

items.title: UNEP: Opportunity has ‘been lost’ to meet 1.5C warming limit without ‘overshoot’
items.summary: A temporary breach of the 1.5C global-warming limit is now “inevitable” following “decades of insufficient climate action”, says the UN… The post UNEP: Opportunity has ‘been lost’ to meet 1.5C warming limit without ‘overshoot’ appeared first on Carbon Brief .

events.article_text:
A temporary breach of the 1.5C global-warming limit is now “inevitable” following “decades of insufficient climate action”, says the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).

In its “sobering” annual assessment of the global “emissions gap”, UNEP says that exceeding the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C limit is “imminent and unavoidable”.

This year’s report, titled “The point of return”, says the “task now” is to minimise the size and scale of a temperature “overshoot” and to “establish a credible return path to 1.5C by the end of the century”.

Even the “lowest possible” overshoot scenario for 1.5C would first see global warming peak at around 1.7-1.8C in the middle of the century before declining, says the report.

This scenario – which is “still aligned with the long-term temperature goal of the Paris Agreement” – would require global emissions cuts of 18% by 2030 and 45% by 2035, while ramping up “removals” of carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere, says UNEP.

In contrast, it notes that the current climate pledges by countries around the world – even if fully implemented – would only reduce emissions by 5-8% by 2030 and 11-15 % by 2035, relative to 2025 levels.

Nonetheless, the report identifies “ample opportunity to accelerate action”, concluding that “countries can still limit peak warming, shorten the duration of overshoot and keep the goals of the Paris Agreement within reach”.

(See Carbon Brief’s detailed coverage of previous reports in 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.)

The report says that emissions in 2025 were “comparable” to those of 2024.

Global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 totalled 58.4bn tonnes of CO2 equivalent (GtCO2e), according to the report. This is around 0.16GtCO2e lower than 2024 levels – albeit, with high levels of uncertainty around the numbers.

In addition, because the figures presented in the 2025 report are “provisional”, the report says, it is “not possible to conclude on the overall direction of emissions in 2025”.

The emissions growth rate has been slowing down in recent decades: the growth rate over 1990-2015 was, on average, 1.7% per year, while emissions have increased by an average of 0.8% per year since 2016.

The chart below shows the total human-driven emissions between 1990 and 2025, separated by greenhouse gas: CO2 from fossil-fuel combustion (dark grey), methane (light grey), nitrous oxide (blue), fluorinated gases (orange) and CO2 from land-use change (green).

Compared to 2024, emissions from fossil fuels increased slightly, by between 0.4-1.1%, says the report. Emissions of both nitrous oxide and fluorinated gases increased by even higher rates, but since these comprise such a small part of total greenhouse gas emissions, “their contribution to the overall trend is relatively less significant”, it adds. Methane emissions remained steady over that time.

A reduction in the CO2 emissions from land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF) “slightly overcompensates” for the rise in emissions of fossil-fuel CO2 and other gases, according to the report. (For more on falling land-use emissions, see Carbon Brief’s explainer.)

The decrease in LULUCF emissions was “partially driven” by a decline in global wildfire emissions, particularly in Africa, South America and parts of south-east Asia. The report notes that these decreases were “likely connected to the ceasing of El Niño conditions”. The ongoing “super” El Niño is likely to cause LULUCF emissions to increase in 2026.

The report also examines countries’ contributions to the increase in greenhouse gas emissions – although here, it excludes LULUCF due to a lag in national-level emissions inventories for the sector.

Among the top six emitters, only the US saw a notable increase in 2025, says the report, whereas emissions in China, the EU, India, Russia and Indonesia were relatively flat. Emissions in the US grew by 133m tonnes of CO2e (MtCO2e) in 2025, due to increased electricity demand and a “rebound” of coal power. This growth in US emissions is likely due to a combination of market factors, including increased heating demand due to a colder winter, higher gas prices and overall increased electricity demand.

The changes for the six largest emitters, the rest of the G20 countries, international transport and the rest of the world can be seen in the chart below.

Across most sectors, progress towards decarbonisation has been “modest”, says the report. The most notable decreases have occurred in the power sector and the transport sector, due to the growth of solar power and electric vehicles. The report notes:

“There are emerging signs of transport sector electrification and decarbonisation, but at rates and levels that are not yet sufficient to drive emissions reductions at the global level.”

However, emissions from the transport sector have continued to grow, due to increased demand for international aviation and shipping.

The report notes that while electricity demand from data centres is “projected to double” by 2030, data centres at present account for less than 1% of total emissions.

All countries were meant to submit new UN climate pledges for 2035, known as the third nationally determined contributions (NDCs) to the Paris Agreement, by February 2025. However, 95% of nations missed this deadline.

Many countries came forward with their third NDCs at a UN climate summit in New York in September 2025 and at the COP30 climate summit in Brazil in November 2025.

By the end of COP30, 122 – or 63% – of countries had produced their third NDCs.

The report says that figure had risen to 124 by 1 September 2026, with pledges now covering 75% of global emissions.

This is more than double the number of third NDCs available at the time of the 2025 emissions gap report – allowing a “more robust basis for assessing collective progress and ambition toward 2035”, says the report.

Although the first global stocktake of action towards the goals of the Paris Agreem

analysis.tldr: A major UN report warns that the world will temporarily cross safe global warming limits, meaning India will likely face more extreme weather that strains agriculture, energy supplies, and insurance costs.
the_story: The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) stated in its annual 'emissions gap' report that a temporary breach of the 1.5C global warming limit is now 'inevitable' and 'imminent'.
Global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 totaled 58.4bn tonnes of CO2 equivalent (GtCO2e), roughly flat compared to 2024.

Among the top six emitters, only the US saw a notable emission increase in 2025 due to higher electricity demand and a rebound in coal power, while emissions in India, China, the EU, Russia, and Indonesia were relatively flat.
Current national climate pledges will only reduce emissions by 5-8% by 2030, falling far short of the 18% cut needed to keep peak warming between 1.7-1.8C and return to 1.5C by 2100.
analysis.what_happened: The UN Environment Programme released its report titled 'The point of return', revealing that decades of insufficient climate action make exceeding the Paris Agreement's 1.5C warming limit unavoidable. Even under the best remaining scenario, global temperatures will temporarily peak around 1.7-1.8C mid-century before coming back down, because current country pledges are too weak to prevent it.
analysis.analogy: It is like a family that spent years ignoring its growing credit card bills; the debt has now grown so large that missing payments entirely is unavoidable, and the only choice left is to tighten the budget drastically to pay it off eventually.
why_it_matters_india: Global failure to cut emissions -> higher peak global temperatures (1.7-1.8C)
Higher global temperatures -> more severe heatwaves, unpredictable monsoons, and extreme weather in India
Extreme weather shocks -> damage to Indian agriculture, driving up food inflation and hurting rural incomes
Stricter global climate scrutiny -> increased pressure on Indian industries to accelerate green transitions, raising near-term costs for power and manufacturing

impacts.rationale: More frequent climate shocks like droughts or floods disrupt crop supplies, raising food prices for ordinary consumers — a bad outcome.
Global pressure to expand renewables like solar will accelerate clean energy investments in India, driving growth for utility firms — generally good for long-term clean infrastructure investors.

watch_next: Updates on India's domestic renewable energy capacity additions and green hydrogen policies
Monsoon forecasts and agricultural output reports regarding extreme weather impacts
analysis.caveats: The report relies on provisional 2025 emissions data with high levels of uncertainty, and future policy shifts by major global economies could alter the pace of warming.

events.headline: Not just AI. China is building technologies that challenge U.S. dominance

items.title: Not just AI. China is building technologies that challenge U.S. dominance
items.summary: From batteries and solar panels to drones and satellites, China is building tech capabilities that extend well beyond AI, writes Steve Feldstein in his new book, "Bytes and Bullets: Global Rivalries, Big Tech, and the New Shape of Modern Warfare."

items.title: How China is building its global EV battery empire
items.summary: An explainer on how China cornered the EV battery market and is now taking its dominance global.

events.article_text:
While China is engaged in a fierce struggle with the U.S. for AI supremacy, it is accelerating its development of other future technologies. In 2024, Chinese investors put nearly $1 trillion in clean-­energy capex for renewables, electricity grids, and energy storage. As a result, China now makes 70% of the world’s EVs, its companies are responsible for 80%–­85% of global solar photovoltaic manufacturing, and they oversee more than 75% of global battery production. Writes Columbia University scholar Tim Wu, “If we set AI aside for a moment and assume that these technologies represent the future, it is clear who is ahead.”

Other benchmarks reach a similar conclusion. Take, for example, the Australian Strategic Policy Institute’s “Critical Technology Tracker,” which analyzes China and the United States’ research capacity across ­74 current and emerging technologies. The latest data from December 2025 indicated that China led research in nearly 90% of crucial technologies, including nuclear energy, synthetic biology, and small satellites. The results revealed a “drastic reversal,” writes Xiaoying You in Nature. At the beginning of the century, American scientists held an enduring advantage in more than 90% of assessed technologies, with China leading in less than 5% of them; but in the intervening 25 years, Chinese researchers flipped the balance.

While the findings are striking, some caveats are in order. Most importantly, the authors measured cited pieces of research as opposed to deployable or applied technology. It is one thing to publish theoretical concepts. It is quite another to come up with a manufacturing process and actually produce specific items. When it comes to innovations like jet engines (a task that remains stubbornly elusive for Chinese engineers), whether research translates to manufacturing is a key question. As the authors acknowledge, “If you’re good at origami but don’t yet excel at making decent paper, are you really good at origami?” Nonetheless, the conclusions are sobering and signify how swiftly China has narrowed the scientific gap with the U.S.

China’s success in the consumer drone industry underscores its growing technological power. Da Jiang Innovations (DJI), which is based in Shenzhen, holds more than 70% of the global consumer drone market. In 2022, the size of that market was about $30.6 billion; it is expected to grow to $55.8 billion by 2030. While studying at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, founder and CEO Frank Wang started DJI in 2006. Rather than work out of a dorm room, Wang and two of his classmates rented a small office across the border in Shenzhen. He started selling drone control systems for hobbyists making their own DIY units. By 2013, DJI released its first preassembled “ready-­to-­fly” drone, the Phantom 1, which sold for less than $700. The product was a hit —­ the cost was reasonable, and the unit came with “serious hardware,” making it stand out from the cheap toy versions being sold at similar price points.

Today, DJI is a behemoth: it has over 14,000 employees and no close competitors. Its drones are ubiquitous, including in the U.S. They are used by first responders to respond to emergencies and by hobbyists to take panoramic photos. They have also become an important fixture on the battlefield, particularly in Ukraine. Both sides rely heavily on DJI drones to surveil troop movements, guide artillery, and identify enemy emplacements. China has reportedly shipped millions of dollars’ worth of DJI units to Russia during the conflict.

But it is not just Wang’s resourcefulness and tenacity that is responsible for DJI’s market dominance. U.S. tech executives confided to me that there was no way a U.S. company could replicate DJI’s success. The industry’s understanding was that DJI scaled due to massive subsidies from the Chinese government, affording it major cost advantages. Reporting from The Washington Post confirmed these claims, despite DJI’s assertions that it had not accepted any funding from the Chinese government. Reporters reviewed company documents and other sensitive information showing that four investment entities “owned or administered by Beijing” invested in DJI, including a government asset manager who played a key role in “promoting partnerships between private enterprises and the Chinese military.”

Not only did state subsidies play an important role in propping up the company, but DJI also benefited from being part of China’s competitive drone ecosystem, which spawned an array of service providers producing advanced components at cut-­rate prices. Few other countries could compete. When a Taiwanese drone manufacturer tried to replace its Chinese-­made engines, it searched far and wide for alternatives, even going to Australia, where it found that an equivalent engine “would cost 20 times more.” The company eventually inked a deal with a local supplier, but only after convincing the bidder to lower its prices “as an act of virtue” to support Taiwan’s defense.

Like other Chinese firms and products (such as TikTok), geopolitics have caught up to DJI. In December 2025, the Federal Communications Commission blacklisted all new foreign-­made drones and components from the U.S. market over concerns that they posed “an unacceptable risk” to national security. While the directive didn’t directly name DJI, given the company’s 80% share of America’s consumer drone market, the implication was clear: DJI drones were no longer welcome in the U.S. (For now, the FCC’s rule doesn’t impact DJI’s unmanned aircraft already in use; it only applies to new drone sales.) In short, today’s geopolitics has made DJI’s position increasingly untenable for America’s interests.

Experts remain divided about how the U.S. and China stack up on science and technology. In certain sectors, American research continues to lead; in other areas, China appears to be supplanting the U.S. What is clear is that the days of China as an “imi

analysis.tldr: China's rapid rise in global clean energy, batteries, and drone manufacturing could reshape global supply chains, impacting raw material costs and trade dynamics for India.
the_story: In 2024, Chinese investors poured nearly $1 trillion into clean-energy capital expenditure (capex) for renewables, electricity grids, and energy storage.
China now produces 70% of the world's electric vehicles (EVs), 80% to 85% of solar photovoltaic manufacturing, and oversees over 75% of global battery production.

Data from December 2025 by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute showed China leads research in nearly 90% of 74 critical and emerging technologies, a complete flip from a 25 years ago when the U.S. led in over 90%.

Shenzhen-based Da Jiang Innovations (DJI) holds over 70% of the global consumer drone market, backed by massive local component ecosystems and, according to reporting, funding from entities administered by Beijing.
In December 2025, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) blacklisted all new foreign-made drones and components over national security risks, targeting market leaders like DJI.
analysis.what_happened: China has massively accelerated its research, manufacturing, and state-backed investments in future technologies like clean energy, batteries, and drones. This was driven by aggressive government subsidies, massive domestic investments totaling nearly $1 trillion in 2024, and the development of highly integrated local manufacturing ecosystems.
analysis.analogy: It is like a rival corner store getting massive financial backing to buy cheaper bulk supplies, allowing them to sell goods way below cost and squeeze out everyone else on the street.
why_it_matters_india: China's dominance in cheap clean-energy components (like solar panels and EV batteries) dictates global prices.
Indian renewable energy and electric vehicle companies rely heavily on imported Chinese equipment and raw materials.
Global trade restrictions, like the U.S. FCC ban on Chinese technology, shift global supply chains and force nations to rethink their vendor dependencies.
Intense technological competition between the U.S. and China shifts global trade flows, impacting raw material costs and manufacturing competitiveness in developing nations like India.

impacts.target: Renewable energy equipment & solar panel import costs in India
impacts.rationale: China's massive production capacity drives down global prices of solar panels and clean tech, which is generally good for Indian renewable energy developers lowering project costs.

impacts.target: EV battery & raw material input costs
impacts.rationale: Overproduction and dominance by Chinese battery giants keep global battery prices low, benefiting Indian electric vehicle makers and consumers.

impacts.target: Indian manufacturing stocks (EV and solar sectors)
impacts.rationale: Cheaper global inputs can help local manufacturing margins, though heavy reliance on Chinese dominance poses long-term strategic risks for local domestic manufacturing firms.

watch_next: Further restrictions or tariffs by Western nations on Chinese clean-tech and hardware
India's domestic policies and production-linked incentives (PLI) for solar cells, batteries, and drones
analysis.caveats: The article notes that measuring research papers and citations does not always translate directly into successful, deployable manufacturing.

history.title: The scam that built India's market plumbing
history.what: A journalist revealed that broker Harshad Mehta had been using forged bank receipts to divert money from the interbank government bond market into shares, driving the Sensex up over 140% in a year. When the mechanism was exposed the index fell roughly 40%.
history.why: The bond settlement system relied on paper receipts and personal trust between banks. There was no electronic record, no central depository, and no regulator with real teeth. Shares settled fortnightly, which let a broker build enormous positions with no money down. The fraud was not clever so much as inevitable given the plumbing.
history.impact: About ₹4,000 crore of public bank money was diverted — enormous for the time. Several bank chairmen were arrested. Retail investors who had bought into the boom lost heavily, and Indian equity took years to recover its reputation with ordinary savers.
history.policy: SEBI, which had existed only as an advisory body, was given statutory powers in 1992. The National Stock Exchange was created as an electronic, screen-based competitor to the broker-controlled BSE. Shares were dematerialised into depositories, and physical certificates disappeared.
history.consequence: This is why buying a share in India today is instant, electronic and safe, settled by a central depository with a regulator behind it — infrastructure that many richer countries took longer to build. The scandal's cost bought the market's plumbing.
history.pattern: Financial scandals almost never come from exotic instruments. They come from a settlement gap, a trust-based process, or a regulator without authority. Ask where the paperwork is manual and who checks it.
history.india_echo: The sequel arrived in 2001 with Ketan Parekh, exploiting the remaining carry-forward settlement system; that ended badla trading and brought in rolling settlement. Two scandals, two upgrades — the pattern of Indian market reform.
history.watch_for: Any market where the same institution executes, settles and audits. The crypto exchange failures of 2022 were this exact structure, rediscovered.
